lesson.title: Putting a Number on the Line: The Correlation Coefficient
lesson.summary: See the full step-by-step computation of the correlation coefficient r for a real data set, and learn what its sign and magnitude do and do not tell you.
lesson.body:
Every earlier idea in this chapter, direction, form, and strength, comes together in a single number called the correlation coefficient, denoted r. For relationships with a linear form, r measures both the direction and the strength of the association in one value that always falls between -1 and 1. A positive r means a positive association, a negative r means a negative association, and the size of r, regardless of sign, tells you how tightly the points cluster around a straight line: values near 1 or -1 indicate a strong linear association, and values near 0 indicate a weak one.

The formula for r essentially standardizes both variables, converting each x-value and y-value into a number of standard deviations from its own mean, multiplies those standardized values together for each point, and averages the result. A computationally convenient version is r = [n(sum of xy) minus (sum of x)(sum of y)], divided by the square root of [n(sum of x squared) minus (sum of x) squared] times [n(sum of y squared) minus (sum of y) squared], where n is the number of pairs. Because it is built from standardized values, r has no units and does not depend on scale, measuring scores out of 100 versus out of 4.0 would not change r, so long as the underlying linear relationship is the same.

Apply this to the study hours and exam score data one more time: (1, 68), (2, 72), (3, 75), (4, 80), (5, 84), (6, 90). Here n = 6, the sum of x-values is 21, the sum of y-values is 469, the sum of x squared is 91, the sum of y squared is 36,989, and the sum of the six xy products is 1717. The numerator is 6(1717) minus 21(469), which is 10,302 minus 9,849, or 453. The first bracket in the denominator is 6(91) minus 21 squared, which is 546 minus 441, or 105. The second bracket is 6(36,989) minus 469 squared, which is 221,934 minus 219,961, or 1,973. Multiplying gives 105 times 1,973, which is 207,165, and its square root is approximately 455.15. Dividing, r equals 453 divided by 455.15, approximately 0.995.

An r of about 0.995 confirms, with a precise number, exactly what the earlier chapters described by eye: this is an extremely strong, positive, linear association. The positive sign matches the positive direction identified earlier, the magnitude, close to 1, matches the tight clustering described in strength of association, and the fact that r is meaningful here at all depends on the linear form confirmed earlier. Change any one of those three properties and the correlation coefficient reported would change to match.

Two cautions matter as much as the calculation itself. First, r only measures linear association, running it on the curved braking distance data from nonlinear form would produce a misleadingly small number even though that relationship is perfectly predictable, just not with a straight line. Second, r measures association, not causation, and it is sensitive to outliers, since one unusual point far from the rest of the data can pull r higher or lower than the other points alone would suggest.

The correlation coefficient is the natural endpoint of the graphical toolkit built across this chapter. You started by flagging an individual unusual point with the 1.5 times IQR rule, then learned to display a distribution's shape and outliers in a modified boxplot and to check for normality with a probability plot, and finally learned to describe a relationship between two variables through direction, form, and strength on a scatterplot. The correlation coefficient closes the loop by turning those visual judgments into a single defensible number.
